core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pheochromocytoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Order CT or MRI of abdomen/adrenals with adrenal protocol, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and severe heart racing for 4 months

Key HPI features: 50F describes 4-month history of sudden, unprovoked episodes lasting 15-30 minutes characterized by throbbing headache, drenching sweats, severe palpitations, and extreme panic. Episodes occur 2-3 times per week.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals (between episodes): HR 76, BP 142/88. Physical exam normal between attacks. Lab screening: Plasma free metanephrines elevated >4x upper limit of normal; 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines markedly elevated.
Relevant background/PMH: Paroxysmal hypertension resistant to standard therapy
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pheochromocytoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Panic disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Blood pressure spikes above 200 systolic during episodes — needs urgent evaluation and careful pre-treatment before any intervention.
management_principles: Order CT or MRI of abdomen/adrenals with adrenal protocol
Initiate mandatory preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade with Phenoxybenzamine (or Doxazosin) for 10-14 days BEFORE initiating any beta-blocker (to prevent hypertensive crisis)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 50F presenting with classic paroxysmal triad of pheochromocytoma: episodic headache, diaphoresis, and tachycardia with severe hypertension.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals (between episodes): HR 76, BP 142/88. Physical exam normal between attacks. Lab screening: Plasma free metanephrines elevated >4x upper limit of normal; 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines markedly elevated.
reference_soap.plan: Order CT or MRI of abdomen/adrenals with adrenal protocol. Initiate mandatory preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade with Phenoxybenzamine (or Doxazosin) for 10-14 days BEFORE initiating any beta-blocker (to prevent hypertensive crisis). Surgical consultation for adrenalectomy.

learning_objectives: Identify the classic symptom triad of pheochromocytoma (headache, sweating, tachycardia)
Select appropriate biochemical screening tests (plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines)
Explain the absolute critical rule of alpha-blockade before beta-blockade in pheochromocytoma

teaching.one_liner: A catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor causing episodic spells of pounding headache, sweating, and severe blood pressure spikes — before surgery, alpha-blockade must be started well before any beta-blocker to avoid a hypertensive crisis.
red_flags: Blood pressure spikes above 200 systolic during episodes — needs urgent evaluation and careful pre-treatment before any intervention

must_ask.say: Can you describe what happens during one of these spells — headache, sweating, racing heart?
How often do these episodes happen, and how long do they last?
How high does your blood pressure go during these spells?
Does anything seem to trigger these episodes?
Does anyone in your family have similar episodes or endocrine tumors?

history.answer: I've been having these terrifying spells where my head pounds terribly, I break out in drenching sweats, and my heart races like crazy.
Each attack comes on very abruptly, reaching its absolute peak within a minute or two without any warning.
These episodes started about four months ago; they happen two to three times every week, which is completely new for me.
The headache is all over my head, but it feels most intense in the back and at the top.
It is a severe, throbbing, pounding pain, easily an eight or nine out of ten while the spell lasts.
Each spell lasts about fifteen to thirty minutes, and then it gradually fades away and I feel completely exhausted.
During every single spell, my chest thumps violently, sweat soaks right through my clothes, and I feel an overwhelming sense of panic.
I checked it with my home cuff during two separate spells, and the monitor read over 210 over 120, which terrified me.
Nothing seems to make the pain better while it is happening, and lying down or changing positions does not help.
No, there are no flashing lights, blind spots, or tingling before the attacks begin.
I feel sick to my stomach during the height of the attack, but I have not thrown up, and bright lights do not bother me.
No, my eyes do not tear up or turn red, my nose does not run, and my eyelids do not droop.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, stiff neck, or rashes at all.
No, I have never had any numbness, weakness on one side, slurred speech, or loss of consciousness.
No, my vision stays clear, with no double vision or eye pain.
No, my temples are not tender, I have no pain when chewing food, and my shoulders and hips do not ache.
No, I have not bumped my head or had any falls or injuries recently.
I tried taking ibuprofen and acetaminophen when the headaches started, but they didn't do anything to stop the attacks.
They seem to strike completely out of nowhere without any obvious trigger like food, stress, or caffeine.
No, nobody else at home or at my school is experiencing headaches, and we do not use gas heaters.
No, I have never had cancer or any immune system issues.
I thought maybe I was having severe panic attacks, or perhaps extreme hot flashes from early menopause.
I am terrified that my blood pressure is spiking above 200 and that I might have a stroke if this continues.
I want to find out what is causing these awful spells and get medicine that will finally make them stop.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure two years ago, but my doctor has had a hard time keeping it under control.
I had an appendectomy when I was twenty, but no other surgeries and no hospital stays since then.
I take lisinopril 20 milligrams and amlodipine 10 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure, and nothing else.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products in my life.
I might have a glass of wine once a month at a dinner, but nothing more than that.
I work as a high school principal and live with my husband; work can be busy, but these spells happen even when I am resting.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke in his seventies, but there is no family history of tumors or endocrine disorders.
My periods have become somewhat irregular over the past year, with my last cycle about two months ago; I am not pregnant and have had a tubal ligation.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg, pulse is 76 beats per minute, respirations are 16 breaths per minute, and temperature is 36.8°C.
Comfortable and alert, not in acute distress, with warm and dry skin and no active sweating or tremors.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; funduscopic examination reveals sharp disc margins without papilledema or vascular changes.
No tenderness upon palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary sinuses.
Supple neck with full active and passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Normal size and texture without nodules, tenderness, enlargement, or bruits.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender without palpable masses; deep palpation does not trigger symptoms.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movements and intact sensation.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout both upper and lower extremities.
Intact sensation to light touch and pinprick symmetrically across all dermatomes.
Intact finger-to-nose testing, smooth rapid alternating movements, steady tandem gait, and negative Romberg sign.
